source_spans.locator: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9(4) (2002), published pp.625-626, abstract and six-claim list: limits on attention/working memory motivate exploiting the environment to reduce cognitive workload, including leaving information externally available and harvesting it on a need-to-know basis

Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9(4) (2002), published p.628, Claim 3 opening: under on-line demands and a representational bottleneck, novel tasks can be handled by strategic external use rather than full internal encoding, including epistemic actions that alter the environment to reduce remaining cognitive work

Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9(4) (2002), published p.629, situated off-loading boundary and examples: long-term archival storage is distinguished from immediate off-loading; Tetris transformations and repeated strategic visual referencing illustrate physical simplification and minimal-memory resampling

Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9(4) (2002), published p.629 and p.635 Conclusions: other attention/working-memory limits can also drive off-loading; symbolic off-loading is a broader, partly off-line extension and is not merged into the bounded situated claim

conditions: situated interaction with task-relevant external information rather than long-term archival storage

novel or otherwise demanding tasks in which time pressure, attention limits, working-memory limits, or related internal processing constraints make full internal encoding, maintenance, or transformation burdensome
task: leave task-relevant information externally available and re-access it as needed
physically transform task-relevant external state to simplify the problem that remains
temporal_scope: during ongoing interaction with a task-relevant external situation

nodes.description: limited internal resources such as attention, working memory, or time available for full encoding, maintenance, or transformation
task-relevant information that remains available in the immediate external environment instead of being fully encoded and maintained internally
physical action that changes task-relevant external state so that less internal computation remains to be performed
need-based re-access of externally available task information, such as strategic repeated visual sampling, instead of maintaining a complete internal copy
internal encoding, maintenance, or transformation work still required after exploiting external task structure

relations.description: limits on internal processing make strategic re-access of external information and problem-simplifying external action useful responses to demanding situated tasks
physically transforming the external task state can simplify the problem and reduce the internal cognitive work remaining to be done
re-accessing task information externally on a need-to-know basis reduces the need to fully encode or continuously maintain that information internally
